analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to give full cash refunds for canceled or badly delayed flights and early ticket cancellations.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required large airlines and ticket sellers to offer passengers a full cash refund when a flight is canceled or significantly delayed, or when the passenger cancels at least 48 hours before departure. Vouchers could still be offered, but only if they never expire and come with a clear notice that cash is available. It also would have let passengers swap unused vouchers from 2020 onward for cash, and required airlines to tell buyers up front that they can cancel for a full cash refund.
analysis.who_benefits: Airline passengers — especially those stuck with a canceled or badly delayed flight who today are often pushed toward a voucher or credit instead of their money back. Under the bill, the refund would cover ancillary fees too, be paid within 30 days of a request, and vouchers offered instead would have to be valid indefinitely and come with a clear notice of the right to cash.

how_it_helps.text: Passengers get a full cash refund — including ancillary fees — within 30 days of requesting it when a large carrier cancels or significantly delays their flight, or when they cancel their own ticket at least 48 hours before departure.

Vouchers can still be offered, but any voucher must remain valid and redeemable indefinitely and must carry a clear, conspicuous notice of the passenger's right to cash — closing the common practice of short-expiration credits.

Passengers holding unused or partially used vouchers from canceled flights since March 2020 could exchange them for cash, and ticket sellers must disclose before purchase that buyers can cancel for a full cash refund.

analysis.who_pays: Large airlines (those with over $1.5 billion in 2019-era operating revenue) and foreign carriers flying to the U.S., which would have to return cash instead of holding it as credits, and ticket agents, who would bear the refund first and seek reimbursement from carriers. Violations carry a $1,000-per-violation civil penalty.

drawbacks.text: The refund is not automatic: it is owed only after the passenger requests it, and only for one flight per city-pair itinerary per date, so travelers who don't know to ask — or who had multi-leg disruptions — could still miss out.

Passengers who cancel less than 48 hours before departure get nothing, and the definition of a 'significant' delay is left to the Transportation Secretary, so the protection's reach depends on future regulation.
The $1,000-per-violation penalty is small relative to airline revenues, and refunding tens of millions of tickets would be a real cost to carriers that could show up partly in fares.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to passengers is concrete and immediate — money back instead of an expiring credit — and the bill deliberately keeps vouchers on the table so airlines retain flexibility. The main weaknesses are that refunds are request-based rather than automatic and that a $1,000 penalty may not deter large carriers. On balance a straightforward pro-consumer bill with modest design gaps.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and an aviation subcommittee the week it was introduced, and neither committee ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 28, 2023 by Rep. Steve Cohen and Rep. Jamie Raskin and referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Financial Services Committee.
On March 1, 2023 it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee, and no further action — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — ever followed.
The bill drew 17 cosponsors, all Democrats, and died with the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 without ever reaching the House floor, let alone the Senate.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large U.S. and foreign passenger airlines are better off: no statute obliges them to return cash for canceled or significantly delayed flights, fund retroactive refunds of 2020-era vouchers, or disclose refund rights before sale. Ticket agents also avoid a fronting-and-reimbursement obligation. Passengers gained nothing from this bill, though the Transportation Department has since written refund rules on its own.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 17 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call shows how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill would force large carriers to return cash for canceled and significantly delayed flights, honor retroactive swaps of 2020-era vouchers, and disclose refund rights up front — money and flexibility airlines currently keep. A $1,000-per-violation penalty is the only cost lever beyond that.

industries.industry: Ticket agents and online travel sellers
industries.note: Agents would have to process refunds first but would be entitled to prompt reimbursement from carriers for the carrier's share, limiting their loss to administrative cost while imposing compliance and disclosure duties.
